extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, judges, policymakers, and others interested in U.S. administrative law and judicial review of agency action
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal standards U.S. courts have used to decide when and how to defer to executive-branch agencies' interpretations of statutes and regulations (the Chevron doctrine and related doctrines), and notes recent changes. Useful for evaluating whether agency interpretations receive judicial deference and on what basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron Step One — Congressional intent clear
rubrics_metrics.description: First question: whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue. If the intent of Congress is clear, that is the end of the matter; the court and the agency must give effect to the unambiguously expressed intent of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the statute unambiguously answers the question, courts must follow the statute and do not defer to the agency; no inquiry into agency reasonableness is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron Step Two — Reasonable/permissible agency construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the statute is silent or ambiguous with respect to the specific issue, the question for the court is whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible (reasonable) construction of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency's interpretation is reasonable/permissible, the court must accept it; only if the agency's construction is unreasonable may the court substitute its own interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative regulations entitled to controlling weight
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress has explicitly left a gap for the agency to fill (an express delegation), legislative regulations promulgated under that delegation are given controlling weight unless they are arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal rulemaking under an express delegation normally commands strong deference, subject to administrative-law validity review (e.g., arbitrary-and-capricious review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit delegation — courts should not substitute their construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the legislative delegation to an agency on a particular question is implicit rather than explicit. In such a case, a court may not substitute its own construction of a statutory provision for a reasonable interpretation made by the administrator of an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without express rulemaking authority, a reasonable agency interpretation filling an implicit gap can still merit judicial deference under Chevron's framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron 'Step Zero' — force of law requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying the Chevron two-step test, courts may ask whether the agency action has the 'force of law' (Chevron 'step zero'). Only agency actions that have the force of law are likely to receive Chevron deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal, notice-and-comment rulemaking is likely to have force of law; informal actions (letters, policy statements, guidance) typically do not and thus may not receive Chevron deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore deference — persuasive weight based on factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Chevron deference does not apply, an agency interpretation may still receive deference under Skidmore: the weight accorded depends upon factors such as the interpretation's consistency with earlier and later pronouncements and its consistency with congressional purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skidmore is a sliding-scale, persuasiveness-based form of deference; courts consider factors like consistency, thoroughness, and fit with statutory purpose when deciding how much weight to give an agency's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auer deference — agency interpretation of its own regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Auer deference is the doctrine of deferring to an agency's interpretation of its own rules and regulations (deference to an agency's reading of its own regulatory text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auer has been limited in various contexts and some jurisdictions or decisions have curtailed or ended Auer-type deference; deference may depend on whether the agency's interpretation is authoritative and within its delegated authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality and form of agency action determine deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The formality and procedural posture of an agency action affect whether and how much deference is due (e.g., notice-and-comment rulemaking more likely to get Chevron; opinion letters, no-action letters, and informal guidance less likely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: a regulation under § 553 notice-and-comment procedures would likely receive Chevron deference; SEC no-action letters or agency letters generally will not and may instead receive Skidmore-type weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine — limits on deference for issues of exceptional significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may decline to apply Chevron deference when the agency's action raises 'major questions'—issues of deep economic and political significance where Congress must have spoken clearly to authorize the agency's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency asserts authority with broad economic or political consequences that is not clearly authorized by Congress, courts may apply the major questions doctrine and refuse deference, treating the matter as one for judicial resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-and-capricious (APA/State Farm) review as a limit on agency rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Even legislative regulations that otherwise merit deference can be set aside if they are arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute (the standard from State Farm under the Administrative Procedure Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts reviewing rulemaking assess whether an agency engaged in reasoned decisionmaking; failure to consider important aspects of the problem or to provide a reasoned explanation can invalidate a rule despite deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency across agency pronouncements as a factor in deference
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative interpretation's weight depends upon 'its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements' of the agency and its fit with congressional purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent postures or ad hoc shifts in interpretation may reduce an agency's claim to deference; consistent, long-standing positions are more persuasive under Skidmore and related analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference inappropriate when challenge targets policy wisdom rather than reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a challenge to an agency construction 'really centers on the wisdom of the agency's policy, rather than whether it is a reasonable choice within a gap left open by Congress, the challenge must fail' under Chevron (i.e., courts should not substitute their policy judgments for the agency's).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should respect legitimate policy choices for matters delegated to agencies, refraining from judicial substitution of policy judgment when the agency's choice is within the permissible range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Loper Bright rule — Chevron overruled (courts choose the 'best reading')
rubrics_metrics.description: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) overruled Chevron, holding that courts should not defer to agencies but should decide the 'best reading' of a law themselves, shifting interpretive authority from agencies to the judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision represents a substantive change: where Chevron formerly required courts to accept reasonable agency constructions, Loper Bright directs courts to independently interpret statutes rather than deferring to agency interpretations. The page notes this reversal and its potential effects on agencies (EPA, OSHA, FDA, CMS) and regulated industries.
